source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: Structure-mapping theory: an analogy is an alignment of relational structure between a base and a target. Object attributes are mostly ignored. Constraints: one-to-one matching, parallel connectivity, and systematicity.
numbers: Theory review; no single effect size. Systematicity: a connected set of relations tied by higher-order relations is a better match than the same number of unconnected matching relations.
quote: Analogies tend to match connected systems of relations
limits: Theory paper. Attribute-light, relation-heavy matching is the definition of a far analogy.
agent_relevance: O7 should ask for the relational skeleton of the source (what causes what, what constrains what), not its surface features, and prefer sources whose relations connect into a system.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: Structure-Mapping Engine (SME): local-to-global. Stage 1 matches identical predicates blindly. Stage 2 merges local matches into structurally consistent clusters (kernels). Stage 3 merges kernels into one or a few best global mappings (normally 2 or 3 interpretations). Candidate inferences then project unmatched base facts onto the target.
numbers: Algorithmic; no accuracy figure in this paper.
limits: Needs rich hand-built predicate representations. Getting such representations from messy design text is the weak point.
agent_relevance: A code-checked mapping step for O7: list source entities and relations, enforce one-to-one pairing, score by connected relation chains, then project candidate inferences back to the problem.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: Cross-mapping shows structure beats objects. When identical objects play different roles in two scenes, people align by relational role, not by object identity (1:3::3:9 pairs the 3s by role).
numbers: Qualitative demonstration; no N in this review.
limits: Cross-mapped pairs are artificial; real design sources rarely have the same object in swapped roles.
agent_relevance: Pair items by role in the relation structure. Guard: a matching surface word must not override a role mismatch.

source: Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer (as summarized in Gentner & Markman 1997)
finding: Retrieval is driven by surface similarity, but judged inferential soundness is driven by shared relational structure. People studied a memory set of stories and were later probed with stories similar in different ways. More shared objects and characters meant more retrieval. More shared causal structure meant higher soundness and similarity ratings. The two came apart.
numbers: Exact N and percentages are not given in the secondary source; the primary paper was not opened.
quote: the kind of similarity that most reliably led to remindings was not the kind participants most valued
limits: Primary not opened. Same retrieval-versus-use split reported for Ross 1987/1989 and Keane 1988; Hammond, Seifert & Gray 1991 is cited as a counter-case.
agent_relevance: Core reason people and models default to near analogues: cheap retrieval favours surface match. O7 must force a separate relational search instead of trusting whichever analogy comes to mind first.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) MAC/FAC (as summarized in Gentner & Markman 1997)
finding: MAC/FAC is a two-stage retrieval model. MAC is a cheap, indiscriminate scan for any kind of similarity. FAC then runs structure-mapping on the few candidates MAC returns. It reproduces surface-heavy remindings with structure-heavy quality judgments.
numbers: Computational model; numbers not in the secondary source.
limits: Primary not opened. Covered in depth by the parallel subfield Analogical retrieval (MAC/FAC); linked here only.
agent_relevance: Pipeline design for an agent: wide cheap recall first, then an expensive structural filter run by code or a counted check.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: Alignable differences are more salient than non-alignable ones and count more against similarity. Time course: with response deadlines under about 700 to 1000 ms, similarity rests on local matches (even cross-mapped object matches). With longer deadlines relational matches take over.
numbers: Time-course claim cited from Goldstone & Medin 1994 and Ratcliff & McKoon 1989; no figures in this review.
limits: Secondary reporting of other studies.
agent_relevance: Quick first-pass similarity judgments favour surface. Any analogy check needs a slow, explicit relational pass.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: Candidate inferences follow the aligned structure. In a story-prediction study people predicted the key fact tied to the matching causal antecedent more than twice as often as the other key fact. Lassaline (1996) found willingness to project new facts rose when they were tied to shared causal relations.
numbers: Ratio: more than 2 to 1. Exact N not given here.
limits: Secondary reporting.
agent_relevance: Accept an inference carried over from the source only if it hangs on relations that were matched. A cheap code-checkable rule for O7.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1980, 1983); Holyoak & Koh (1987); Ross (1987, 1989) transfer studies (as reported in Ding et al. 2023 and Gentner & Markman 1997)
finding: On Duncker's radiation problem people are much more likely to retrieve analogues about cancer or radiation than the structurally matching story of an army splitting up to attack. Retrieval favours near, within-domain sources; successful transfer depends on structure.
numbers: Original percentages (solving rates without and with a hint) were not read in a primary source this session.
limits: Primary papers not opened; claim taken from two opened secondary sources.
agent_relevance: Without an explicit prompt to use the source, a distant analogy is likely to be ignored. The scaffold should make using the analogy an explicit step.

source: Fu, Chan, Cagan, Kotovsky, Schunn & Wood (2013) The meaning of near and far (as reported in Luo, Sarica & Wood 2021)
finding: With patents as stimuli and analogical distance measured by latent semantic analysis, nearer patents stimulated ideas more effectively despite limited novelty, and patents analogically very far from the problem were ineffective as inspiration.
numbers: No figures read; the primary article was not opened.
limits: Secondary report only. It does not support the simple claim that farther is always better. The primary (Fu 2013) was later read: see a32.
agent_relevance: Do not just maximise distance. The target is near-in-purpose, far-in-mechanism (see Hope et al.).

source: Student patent-search experiment with 100+ engineering students (reported in Luo, Sarica & Wood 2021)
finding: Students designing a spherical rolling robot searched patents freely. Over 200 concepts resulted. Patents from nearer fields were more likely to inspire and gave higher-quality ideas. Patents from farther fields gave more novel inspiration.
numbers: N over 100 students, over 200 concepts; knowledge distance computed between patent classes.
quote: nearer to the target domain are more likely to inspire designers and stimulate ideas with higher quality
limits: Self-selected stimuli, patents only, one task. Reported by the authors who then built the tool, a possible bias. Primary experiment not opened.
agent_relevance: Trade-off to encode: near sources raise feasibility and quality, far sources raise novelty. Make distance an explicit dial chosen by goal, with a feasibility check on far ideas.

source: Luo, Sarica & Wood (2021) Guiding data-driven design ideation by knowledge distance
finding: An expert system uses a network of all patent technology fields. Knowledge distance between fields is estimated from patent co-classification statistics and used to retrieve near-field or far-field stimuli for analogy or combination, at three levels: terms, documents and fields.
numbers: Two case studies (rolling toy; open-ended innovation). No controlled comparison with a baseline.
quote: far-field stimuli contribute to novelty
limits: Case studies only. No effect size. The tool authors evaluate their own tool.
agent_relevance: A concrete way to put a number on near versus far: a computed distance between domains, used by code to pick sources.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur & Shahaf (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining
finding: Learned purpose and mechanism vectors from product descriptions find analogies with higher precision and recall than TF-IDF and other baselines. The target is near in purpose, far in mechanism, chosen by a MAX-MIN diversification over mechanism distance.
numbers: Test pairs N = 2500 (training on about 5500 products). The proposed model beat the baselines across all top-K levels in Table 2.
quote: approach outperformed the baselines
limits: Product-description domain; crowd-made purpose and mechanism labels; baselines are simple bag-of-words.
agent_relevance: A recipe for O7: state the purpose and the mechanism of the problem separately, then search for the same purpose with a different mechanism.

source: Hope et al. (2017) ideation experiment
finding: Within-subjects ideation test: 38 Mechanical Turk workers redesigned products (12 seed products) under three conditions: purpose-mechanism analogies, TF-IDF (near, surface) and random (far, irrelevant). The analogy condition produced the most good ideas.
numbers: 749 ideas in total. Liberal rule (at least 2 of 5 judges): 249 good. On the 9 seeds in all conditions, share good: 46% (N=105) analogy, 37% random (49), 30% TF-IDF (54), p<=.01. Strict rule (3 of 5): 38% vs 22% random vs 21% TF-IDF. Model estimate pr(good) 0.71 [0.48, 0.87] vs 0.28 TF-IDF and 0.27 random (B=-1.81 and -1.88, p<.01). Fleiss kappa 0.51.
quote: Participants are significantly more likely to generate good ideas
limits: Small sample, wide confidence intervals (the authors say a replication may land between), crowd workers not designers, good defined by the authors, no replication found this session.
agent_relevance: Random (far, irrelevant) did about as badly as near-surface TF-IDF, so far alone does not help. Relevance of purpose plus difference in mechanism is what matters.

source: Ding, Srinivasan, MacNeil & Chan (2023) Fluid transformers and creative analogies
finding: Prompt exploration with GPT-3 for cross-domain analogies to six design problems (480 analogies). One-shot prompts gave the best mix of usefulness and distance. Zero-shot outputs stayed close to the input problem and often duplicated.
numbers: Table 1 (potential usefulness, duplicate rate, unique-and-useful rate, mean semantic similarity to problem): zero-shot 0.68, 0.24, 0.43, 0.72; one-shot (manager example) 0.82, 0.12, 0.70, 0.48; one-shot (Duncker example, verification run) 0.80, 0.03, 0.77, 0.43; few-shot 0.67, 0.02, 0.65, 0.31.
quote: one-shot outputs were judged to be consistently more potentially useful
limits: One researcher judged usefulness. Old model (GPT-3 davinci). Duplicates only visible at set level.
agent_relevance: Left alone an LLM drifts to near analogies (similarity 0.72). A worked example in the prompt lowers similarity to about 0.45 and raises unique useful output. Embedding similarity to the problem is a code check on analogy distance.

source: Ding et al. (2023) Study 1: use-time test
finding: Participants reformulated a design problem after seeing a GPT-3 analogy. Median helpfulness was 4 of 5. Reformulations mostly added information (84.09%) and rarely rejected parts of the original framing (10.45%).
numbers: Prolific: 123 recruited, 110 analysed, 220 analogy-response pairs. Adding 185/220; rejecting 23/220; both 22/220. Second analogy rated higher than the first (median 4 vs 3; Wilcoxon p=0.002). Helpfulness correlated with adding (r_pb=0.2559, p=0.0001) but not with rejecting (r_pb=0.0094, p=0.8891).
limits: Helpfulness was self-rated, not a measure of final design quality. No human-made-analogy control arm.
agent_relevance: Analogies rarely made people drop their frame. Add-versus-reject is a measurable outcome the agent could track.

source: Ding et al. (2023) predictability and harm
finding: A researcher's a-priori judgment of an analogy's usefulness did not predict how helpful participants found it in use. Harm screening found an upper bound of about 25% of outputs potentially harmful, with 80% of those merely upsetting rather than biased or toxic.
numbers: Correlation of a-priori usefulness with in-use helpfulness r_pb=-0.0266, p=0.6939. Harm upper bound 25% (28/108 = 26% in the text).
limits: One rater's prediction was used, so the null may reflect a poor rater, as the authors note.
agent_relevance: Usefulness of an analogy is hard to judge before use. Judge it by whether it changes the problem representation or passes a held-out check (G3), not by plausibility.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat human college students on text matrix reasoning, letter-string analogies and four-term verbal analogies. It showed the human pattern of worse performance when analogs are semantically distant.
numbers: Letter strings: N=57 UCLA undergraduates. Verbal analogy: N=57 (UCLA VAT) and N=20 (Sternberg & Nigro). Jones et al. set: semantic distance effect for GPT-3 OR=3.24, p=0.0165, CI [1.24, 8.5].
quote: GPT-3 displayed a surprisingly strong capacity for abstract pattern induction
limits: Later shown fragile on counterfactual versions (a20). Possible training-data exposure of the tasks.
agent_relevance: LLMs have real analogy capacity, but humans and models both degrade with semantic distance, so far analogies need extra scaffolding.

source: Webb et al. (2023) story analogies, near versus far
finding: Using Gentner et al. story materials: humans and GPT-3 both chose the target that shares causal structure in the near condition (literal similarity vs mere appearance). In the far condition (true vs false analogy) only humans were reliably above chance.
numbers: Humans N=54: near t(53)=21.5, far t(53)=16.7, both p<1e-22. GPT-3 binomial: near p=0.0039, far p=0.065 (not significant). Humans beat GPT-3: OR=0.37, p=0.0003; 15/54 humans chose the analogous story every trial. GPT-4 (preliminary): nearly perfect near; above chance far (p=0.0039).
limits: GPT-4 test was preliminary. Stories were short and hand-built.
agent_relevance: The near/far gap appears in the LLM exactly where design needs it. Far analogies are where models are weakest, so verify far mappings.

source: Webb et al. (2023) analogical problem solving, radiation problem
finding: On Duncker's radiation problem GPT-3 used an analogous story to find the convergence solution. With distractor stories in context it failed, as people do, but succeeded again when told to consider the earlier stories.
numbers: Qualitative transcripts in the supplement; no percentages.
quote: GPT-3 displayed these same effects
limits: Single-problem demonstration.
agent_relevance: An explicit cue to consider the earlier cases unlocks the right source from a mixed context. Use it as a scaffold step.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Failed generalisation of Webb et al. On counterfactual letter-string problems (permuted alphabets, symbols) humans stayed high while GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 dropped sharply.
numbers: Mean accuracy over all counterfactual alphabets and problem types: humans 0.753 [0.734, 0.773] (1,876 samples, 136 Prolific participants); GPT-3 0.488; GPT-3.5 0.350; GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each).
quote: these models lack the robustness and generality of human analogy-making
limits: Letter strings are an idealised domain; only 2023 models tested.
agent_relevance: Success on familiar analogy forms can reflect memory. Test the agent's analogies on mutated, unfamiliar variants (G3).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting: the model first writes 3 to 5 relevant problems with solutions, then solves the target. It beat 0-shot chain-of-thought and often manual few-shot CoT.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-3.5-turbo 77.8% vs 0-shot CoT 75.8% vs 5-shot CoT 76.7%; PaLM2 81.7% vs 78.2% vs 80.7%; text-davinci-003 61.0% vs 50.3% vs 54.0%. MATH: 37.3% (GPT-3.5) vs 33.9% vs 34.9%. Codeforces Acc@1: GPT-4 19% (knowledge plus exemplars) vs 16% 0-shot CoT vs 17% 3-shot; GPT-3.5-16k 15% vs 9% vs 11%.
limits: Gains are small (1 to 2 points on GSM8K). These are near analogues (same task type), not far design-style transfer. Fails when the new problem is harder than the generated ones.
agent_relevance: Evidence that self-generated analogous problems help strong models, but this is near-analogy transfer.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) ablations on model scale and number of exemplars
finding: With small models, fixed or retrieved labelled exemplars beat self-generated ones. With text-davinci-002 and -003 self-generation wins. One exemplar (K=1) hurts because the model leans on it; K of 3 or 5 is best.
numbers: Best K = 3 or 5 on GSM8K and MATH.
quote: self-generation fails to produce useful or valid exemplars
limits: OpenAI and PaLM-era models only.
agent_relevance: If the agent's model is small, retrieve analogies from a store. Ask for several (3 or more) diverse analogies, never one.

source: Bhavya, Xiong & Zhai (2022) Analogy generation by prompting large language models
finding: InstructGPT can generate meaningful analogous concepts. Quality rises with model size and is sensitive to prompt style (imperative statements beat questions) and temperature.
numbers: Human evaluation of 1,407 analogies, 3 workers each. Share rated meaningful, no-source setting: 0.3B 1.90%, 1.3B 15.61%, 6.7B 48.29%, 175B 70.05%, human reference 66.67%. With a source concept given: 8.97%, 29.05%, 38.46%, 53.79% vs human 71.88%.
quote: largest InstructGPT model can achieve human-level performance
limits: Science-teaching analogies, not design. Meaningful is a weak criterion.
agent_relevance: Model size matters a lot; weak models restate the definition instead of producing an analogy.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy
finding: A corpus of 24K story pairs annotated with entity similarity and relation similarity (Gentner's structure-mapping extended). Choosing the best analogy among options is far below human level, and models are pulled by surface similarity.
numbers: Multiple choice, chance 25%: humans 85.7%; ChatGPT about 30%; best LLM about 48% (gap 37.7 points); FlanT5-xxl 41 to 48%. In a hard-negative test the paper says target choice was under 20% against 50% chance.
quote: models prioritize surface similarity over structural similarity
limits: Stories partly LLM-generated; crowd annotation.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that LLMs confuse surface and relational match, the skill O7 needs. Do not trust the model to say which source is structurally closest.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) Beneath surface similarity: SCAR
finding: Benchmark of 400 scientific system analogies from 13 fields that requires a one-to-one concept mapping (structure abduction). Word-analogy scores overstate analogical skill.
numbers: Average accuracy with 1-shot plus background: GPT-4 69.10, ChatGPT 65.87, InstructGPT-003 49.66; humans 86.03. GPT-4 1-shot on a word-analogy mean: 83.99. Low overlap between word-analogy success and structure success.
quote: LLMs often overlook the structures that underpin these analogies
limits: Human baseline from two graduate students; bilingual table, figures read from a messy text extract.
agent_relevance: Word-level analogy skill does not mean the model can map systems. Require explicit mapping tables with checks.

source: Zhu & McComb (2022) Biologically inspired design concept generation using generative pre-trained transformers
finding: GPT-3 fine-tuned on 221 AskNature bio-inspired design samples generates bio-inspired concepts, with trained relevancy evaluators. For a lightweight flying car, over 50% of generated analogies were birds, then insects, the near attribute-similar source.
numbers: Training: 221 positive samples (442 per evaluator with negatives). Engineers rated novelty and feasibility; 9 of 10 returned surveys usable. Looser problem prompts (Type 1, 2) gave higher novelty and lower feasibility; the strict one (Type 3) more feasible and less novel.
quote: generators are over 50% likely to retrieve birds as an analogy
limits: Small team evaluation, one case study.
agent_relevance: The model reproduces the human near-analogy bias even after fine-tuning. Add an instruction to exclude the obvious domain, and expect looser framing to give more novel but less feasible ideas.

source: Zhu, Zhang & McComb (2022) Generative pre-trained transformers for biologically inspired design (preprint)
finding: Earlier preprint of the same approach: three concept generators defined by how loosely the problem space is represented, plus machine evaluators of domain relevance.
numbers: See a26 for the numbers.
limits: Preprint overlapping a26.
agent_relevance: Same lessons as a26; counted once.

source: Li, Zhang, Cao & Chen (2026) Beyond input-output: design-by-analogy in human-AI collaboration (CHI 26)
finding: Systematic review of 85 studies of AI-driven design by analogy. Six forms of representation (semantics and text; visual and appearance; material and structure; function and attribute; interaction and experience; unconventional contexts), seven stages of the creative process, and four computational stages (representation, retrieval, mapping, evaluation). Most systems rely on text.
numbers: 85 studies reviewed (41 systems tabulated in one figure); six representations; seven stages; three application domains.
quote: Design-by-Analogy ... roots in Gentner's Structure-Mapping Theory
limits: Review with no pooled effect size. Claims about reduced fixation come from cited primary work not re-checked here.
agent_relevance: A map of the design space: analogy needs a representation step, retrieval, mapping and evaluation. Evaluation is the thinnest part.

source: Linsey, Markman & Wood (2012) WordTree; Chan et al. (2011) analogical distance, commonness and modality; Linsey et al. (2010) fixation (cited in Li et al. 2026 and Ding et al. 2023)
finding: Named in the opened sources as the human-subject core of design by analogy: WordTree (re-represent the problem as function words, then search linked words for analogies), Chan et al. on ideation by analogical distance, commonness and modality of examples, and Linsey et al. on fixation. No underlying numbers were read.
numbers: Not read. The primary articles are paywalled and every search channel was rate-limited in this session.
limits: Chan 2011 and Fu 2013 are read in a31 and a32. WordTree (Linsey 2012) and Linsey 2010 fixation are still not read.
agent_relevance: Treat the near-versus-far design effect sizes as unverified until the primary papers are read.

source: Marshall, Crawford & Jensen (2016) analogy-seeded mind-maps (as listed in Li et al. 2026)
finding: Listed as a comparison of verbal versus pictorial representation of analogies in concept generation. No results were read.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Reference only.
agent_relevance: Representation (words versus pictures) of the analogy is an open design variable; a text-only agent is limited to the verbal form.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood & Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design (J. Mech. Des. 133(8))
finding: 2x2x2 experiment with senior engineering students designing a low-cost human-motion energy harvester. Far-field patent examples (vs near-field) raised novelty and the spread of quality, and were used more (solution transfer). Less-common examples helped more than common ones. Picture versus text made no difference. Far-field cost about one idea of quantity.
numbers: N=153 students, 1,321 ideas; distance x commonness x modality plus a no-example control (N=24). Distance on solution transfer: far > near, d=0.60 (eta2 0.08). Mean and max novelty: far > near, d=0.56, p<.05. Variability of quality: far > near d=0.64 and far > control d=0.78, p<.05. Quantity: far < near d=-0.30. Mean and max quality: no distance effect. Far vs control on novelty was not significant alone; only far plus less-common beat control. More-common examples cut quantity (d=-0.67 vs less-common, -0.76 vs control) and breadth (d=-1.03 vs control).
quote: positive effects of far-field and less-common examples on novelty and variability in quality of solution concepts
limits: One design problem; two examples per cell; novices not experts; early ideation only, no finished designs. The quantity cost vanished once time spent mapping the example was removed (p=0.47), so it is a mapping cost.
agent_relevance: Founding positive result for far analogues: they raise novelty and variance, not mean quality. Pair far sources with a selection step that keeps the high-quality tail, and budget tokens for mapping them.

source: Fu, Chan, Cagan, Kotovsky, Schunn & Wood (2013) The meaning of near and far (J. Mech. Des. 135(2))
finding: A second experiment, with distance defined by position in a structure of patents (latent semantic analysis plus a structural-form algorithm), found the opposite of Chan 2011: near patents did better than far. Reconciled as a sweet spot: stimuli labelled near in Chan 2011 were too near, and stimuli labelled far here were too far.
numbers: 72 recruited (70 analysed): 24 near (0 or 1 node away), 24 far (3 nodes away), 24 control; 3 of 5 patents per participant. Mean quality F(2,65)=4.07, p=0.02: near > far d=0.76, p=0.02; near vs control d=0.54, p=0.23 (n.s.). Max quality F(2,65)=4.13, p=0.02; far < near d=-0.76; far vs control d=-0.72, p=0.11 (n.s.). Far patents rated less relevant: F(1,44)=4.72, p=0.035, d=-0.64.
quote: there is such a thing as too far
limits: Two similar-protocol studies by the same group, same problem and metrics. The sweet-spot account is post hoc and the authors say its position depends on the patents and problem. Novices. The between-study comparison is not randomised.
agent_relevance: Distance is not monotone: near and far are relative. Pick sources by a measured distance band, check relevance to the problem, and avoid random inspiration (authors argue random stimuli are often too far).

source: Chan, Dow & Schunn (2015) Do the best design ideas (really) come from conceptually distant sources of inspiration? (Design Studies 36)
finding: Field data from OpenIDEO. Citing any source goes with more creative concepts, but closer sources, not farther ones, were more beneficial. The inverse distance-creativity relation held across design problems. A challenge to the claim that the best ideas build on the farthest sources.
numbers: 2,341 concepts in 12 challenges by 1,190 contributors citing 4,557 unique inspirations; 707 concepts (357 authors) cited at least one of 2,245 inspirations; 110 of those were shortlisted (about 16%) vs 241 (10%) of all concepts.
quote: conceptually closer rather than farther sources appear more beneficial
limits: Observational, not randomised; what people choose to cite is self-selected; distance from text analysis; the outcome is an expert shortlist, which mixes novelty with feasibility; real teams over weeks, not 30-minute lab tasks.
agent_relevance: Strong counter-evidence to far-is-best over long realistic work. Do not hard-code a far-analogy preference; make the distance dial depend on the goal and test both.

source: Chan & Schunn (2015) far analogies and concept jumps in a professional design team (Cognitive Science; abstract read from a shared scratch file)
finding: In a professional team's brainstorming, concepts were more similar to the preceding concept after a far analogy than at baseline, not less. Yet far analogies raised the concept generation rate. This rejects the jump account of far analogies and suggests deeper, iterative exploration within a functional space.
numbers: Abstract only was read; specific counts were not extracted.
quote: concepts were more similar to their preceding concepts after far analogy use
limits: One team, in vivo; a surprising result from a single case; abstract-level reading only. The file title did not match this abstract exactly, so verify the citation.
agent_relevance: Far analogies may work by opening one new region for sustained exploration rather than one big leap. A loop that keeps developing the analogy for several steps may beat a one-shot far analogy.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson & Gentner (1999) Analogical encoding facilitates knowledge transfer in negotiation
finding: Comparing two cases that embody the same principle, and stating the shared principle, led to much more transfer than studying the same cases separately.
numbers: Experiment 2: graduate management students who drew an analogy from two cases were nearly three times more likely to use the training strategy in a later negotiation than students given the same cases separately. Experiment 1: undergraduates with analogy training proposed more optimal strategies and fewer compromises.
quote: nearly three times more likely to incorporate the strategy
limits: Negotiation context; only the abstract and introduction were read. Linked to the parallel subfield Transfer of learning.
agent_relevance: Operational recipe: give the agent two sources and have it state what they share before applying anything. Comparison of two cases beats one case.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024b) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Extended test of Webb et al. on letter strings, digit matrices and story analogies with variants unlikely to be in training data. Humans stayed high on two letter-string variants while GPT models fell sharply. Digit matrices showed the drop on one of two variants. Complex analogies were hard for both.
numbers: Abstract-level reading; figures not extracted.
limits: Abstract read only; models from 2023 and 2024.
agent_relevance: Reinforces that apparent analogical skill in LLMs partly reflects familiarity; use variants and held-out checks.
